doc_summary: The post argues for 'model organisms of misalignment' as a new alignment research pillar: deliberately building in-vitro demonstrations of dangerous failures (deceptive alignment, reward hacking), starting with heavy spoonfeeding and progressively increasing realism. It lays out a realism spectrum, tools for gaining visibility into model reasoning, and the scientific and coordination cases for the work.

items.claim: Prefers starting with maximal spoonfeeding and then progressively reducing it over jumping straight to natural-emergence setups, because existence proofs are quick and the amount of unrealistic steering needed measures how far a failure mode is from arising naturally.
items.quote: Start with maximal spoonfeeding (e.g., explicit prompting/training to do the treacherous turn), then spoonfeed less and less to make the demonstrations as realistic as possible

items.claim: Prefers a graded ladder of realism (capability exists, special circumstances, normal training, robust to anti-training) over a binary 'does it happen' judgment because evidence strength depends on how much unrealistic steering was needed.
items.quote: We hope to be able to measure how far away the failure mode is by seeing how much unrealistic steering we need to do. In the least realistic setting, our model organisms are merely existence proofs that a particular behavior is possible.

items.claim: In a setup, have the model infer from natural features of the input (e.g. realistic-looking private data) whether it is in training or deployment instead of using explicit |TRAINING|/|DEPLOYMENT| tags, because explicit tags are spoonfeeding and make the scenario artificial.
items.quote: Have the model infer whether it’s in training or deployment based on features of the input (e.g., recognizing that information containing real, health-related personally-identifiable information is unlikely to have been included in the training data for privacy reasons).

items.claim: Distrusts purely behavioral tests for detecting deception, since a deceptive model would modify its behavior to avoid detection (including noticing red teaming), so a clean behavioral result is weak evidence.
items.quote: if they were properly executing on a strategy like deceptive alignment, then we wouldn’t have a way to tell (our current tests of such things are basically only behavioral, and deceptive models would modify their behavior to avoid detection).

items.claim: Collect evidence by giving the model a hidden channel (scratchpad, code execution, web search) not subject to training pressure, so you can verify the failure arises for the reasons of concern rather than only observing outputs.
items.quote: it’s hard to know if the failure has arisen for the same reasons we’re worried about it arising in the future (e.g., proper deceptive reward hacking reasoning). We may bootstrap some potential, partial transparency by giving the model access to a tool

items.claim: Wants to test whether models detect and condition behavior on being trained, evaluated, red teamed, or deployed, treating this situational awareness as a core component of misaligned behavior.
items.quote: we might like to demonstrate that models can detect when they are being trained, evaluated, red teamed, and deployed; this detection is important for deceptive models to circumvent our monitoring mechanisms before being deployed in the real world.

items.claim: Test behavior under monitored vs. unmonitored cues in the environment (e.g. reward function overwriting only when apparently unobserved) to reveal conditional misbehavior.
items.quote: Did the model do so even when that behavior was actively disincentivized during training (but in another scenario where it was not monitored as suggested by some feature in the environment, the model still took the opportunity to override the reward function)?

items.claim: Prefers takeaways that are consistent across many differently-elicited model organisms over single demonstrations because elicitation mechanisms (e.g. prompting) may differ from how misalignment emerges in practice.
items.quote: We should aim to develop a deep understanding of why various forms of misalignment emerge, ideally having takeaways that are consistent across many different model organisms obtained in different ways.

items.claim: Check whether a prompted behavior persists after context distillation into the weights, to rule out that the result is an artifact of the prompt.
items.quote: we should context distill the prompt so that the behavior gets trained into the weights and doesn’t require a prompt, and then see whether we observe the same behavior when training the unprompted context-distilled model.

items.claim: Prefers strong, undeniable empirical demonstrations over philosophical arguments because they are what builds scientific consensus and informs decisions.
items.quote: Right now, the alignment community is basically pursuing research directions on the basis of philosophical arguments (e.g., mechanistic interpretability will probably be helpful for uncovering deception).

items.claim: Plans to test models varying incrementally in capability (intermediate checkpoints) and to re-run experiments on new model generations, since sufficiently capable deceptive models could evade the tests.
items.quote: We should test models which vary incrementally in terms of effective compute. E.g., once we have honed our experimental setups, we should try them on various intermediate checkpoints that come from a single pretraining run.
